questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. What does $L_{k-1}$ count?
options: The number of jobs that arrive during period $k-1$ only.
The number of jobs present at the start of period $k$.
The number of jobs that depart at the end of period $k$.
The number of jobs present at the end of period $k+1$.

questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. If jobs that arrive in period $k$ cannot be served in that period and service is work-conserving, what is $d_k$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. In the departure rule $d_k=\min\{L_{k-1}+a_k,c_k\}$, what is the role of the minimum?
options: It prevents the server from serving more jobs than are present.
It ensures that the queue length never exceeds the capacity $c_k$.
It chooses whichever of arrivals or capacity is larger in period $k$.
It makes the server idle whenever new jobs arrive in period $k$.

questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. Which information is enough to construct the whole sequence $L_1,L_2,\dots,L_n$ with the recursion?
options: The individual inter-arrival times and service times of every job.
The averages $\bar a$ and $\bar c$ of arrivals and capacity per period.
The sequences $\{a_k\}$ and $\{c_k\}$; the start $L_0$ does not matter.
The start $L_0$ together with the sequences $\{a_k\}$ and $\{c_k\}$.

questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. In this model jobs are not counted as being 'in service'. What does that imply about $L_k$?
options: $L_k$ counts only jobs that will depart in period $k+1$.
$L_k$ is both the number in the system and the number in queue.
$L_k$ equals the number in queue plus $c_k$ jobs in service.
$L_k$ is the number in system minus the departures $d_k$.

questions.question: In a discrete-time queue where jobs arriving in period $k$ can be served in that period, $L_k=[L_{k-1}+a_k-c_k]^+$, where $x^+=\max\{x,0\}$, $L_k$ is the number at the end of period $k$, $a_k$ the arrivals and $c_k$ the capacity. With $L_{k-1}=1$, $a_k=2$ and $c_k=5$, what is $L_k$?

Two stations work in series: the jobs that leave station 1 in period $k$ arrive at station 2 in the same period, $a^2_k=d^1_k$. At both stations a job can be served in its arrival period, so $d^i_k=\min\{L^i_{k-1}+a^i_k,c^i_k\}$ and $L^i_k=L^i_{k-1}+a^i_k-d^i_k$. With $L^1_{k-1}=4$, $a^1_k=2$, $c^1_k=3$, $L^2_{k-1}=1$ and $c^2_k=2$, what is $L^2_k$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. A queue starts with $L_0=4$ jobs, receives $\sum_{k=1}^{10}a_k=30$ jobs in ten periods and ends with $L_{10}=7$. How many jobs departed in these ten periods in total?

One machine with capacity $c_k=6$ jobs per period serves queue 1 with priority over queue 2; new jobs wait for the next period, and service is work-conserving. At the start of period $k$ queue 1 holds $4$ jobs and queue 2 holds $5$. How many queue-2 jobs depart in period $k$?

The function `queue_lengths(a, c, L0)` builds $L_0,L_1,\dots$ with $d_k=\min\{L_{k-1}+a_k,c_k\}$ and $L_k=L_{k-1}+a_k-d_k$, returning the list starting with $L_0$. What does it return for arrivals $(1,4,0)$, capacities $(2,2,2)$ and $L_0=1$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. Let $L_k$ follow the version where new jobs wait for the next period and $L'_k$ the version where they can be served on arrival, with the same $L_0$, $\{a_k\}$ and $\{c_k\}$. Which relation holds?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. When new jobs cannot be served in their arrival period, $L_k=L_{k-1}-\min\{L_{k-1},c_k\}+a_k$. Which expression equals this for all non-negative integers $L_{k-1}$, $a_k$, $c_k$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. The recursion gives the sequences $\{L_k\}$ and $\{d_k\}$. What else must be specified before the waiting times of individual jobs can be determined?
options: A constant capacity $c_k=c$ in every single period.
The order of service, for example first-in-first-out.
An arrival count $a_k$ of at most $c_k$ in every period.
Nothing more, since each job waits $L_k/c_k$ periods.

questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. Capacity varies by period and a job may leave in the period it arrives. Starting from $L_0=5$, with arrivals $(a_1,a_2)=(4,6)$ and capacities $(c_1,c_2)=(6,3)$, how many jobs remain after two periods, $L_2$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. New jobs wait for the next period, service is work-conserving, $L_0=0$, arrivals are $(3,0,2)$ and $c_k=2$ in each of the three periods. How many units of capacity are unused in total over the three periods?

In a discrete-time queue where jobs arriving in period $k$ can be served in that period, $L_k=[L_{k-1}+a_k-c_k]^+$, with $L_k$ the number at the end of period $k$, $a_k$ the arrivals and $c_k$ the capacity. If $L_{k-1}=2$, $c_k=4$ and $L_k=5$, how many jobs arrived in period $k$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. From the same $L_{k-1}$, compare the update $[L_{k-1}-c_k]^++a_k$ (new jobs wait) with $[L_{k-1}+a_k-c_k]^+$ (new jobs served on arrival). For non-negative integers, exactly when do the two give the same $L_k$?

A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. When new jobs wait for the next period, $d_k=\min\{L_{k-1},c_k\}$, so capacity can stay unused although $a_k>0$ jobs are in the system. Is this service work-conserving?
options: No, because capacity is idle while jobs are present in the system.
Yes, because capacity is idle only when no job may be served.
Yes, because $d_k=c_k$ holds in every period of this version.
No, it is work-conserving only in periods where $a_k=0$.

questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. Over $50$ periods the arrivals total $\sum_{k=1}^{50}a_k=600$, the capacities total $\sum_{k=1}^{50}c_k=500$, and $L_0=0$. Which statement about $L_{50}$ holds under either timing convention, whatever the individual $a_k$ and $c_k$?
options: $L_{50}\le 100$, since some capacity may stay unused.
$L_{50}\ge 100$, since at most $500$ jobs can depart.
Only $L_{50}\ge 0$, since just the totals are given.

questions.question: A discrete-time queue has, in period $k$, arrivals $a_k$, capacity $c_k$ (maximal number served), departures $d_k$, and $L_k$ jobs at the end of period $k$. New jobs wait for the next period, $L_0=0$, arrivals are $(2,1,3,0)$ and $c_k=2$ in each of the four periods. What is the average queue length $\bar L=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^{4}L_k$?
